paras: The Brooksville courthouse shooting was a clash at the Hernando County courthouse in Brooksville, Florida, on the afternoon of June 29, 1882, in which white townspeople shot and killed three Black brothers, Henry, Jim and Rube Turner. Several other Black men were wounded and two or more white men were slightly hurt. Carried nationally from Jacksonville under headlines such as "Conflict of Races" and "A War of Races," the story was told entirely from the white side and blamed the Turners for the fight.

According to a Brooksville letter to the Jacksonville Union, the trouble began when a young white man named Stringfellow pushed a Black man, Tom Johnson, aside in Hancock's barroom, and Jim Turner then knocked Stringfellow down and cut his head with a pistol. Jim Turner was arrested, but the case was dismissed for want of evidence; on the following days Marshal Hancock arrested Rube and Henry Turner and a white man, Mr. Quinn, after the brothers drew a pistol and a gun on him. The first dispatch from Brooksville said the Turners had come to town armed on Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday and "threatened to kill a number of our citizens."

By Wednesday afternoon at least fifty Black men were in town, and on Thursday morning the correspondent counted between fifty and seventy-five, all armed. The white residents "began to make preparations," and the mayor appointed five or six special police to aid the marshal and his deputy.

As the marshal was calling the afternoon session of court, Jim and Henry Turner entered the courthouse, Henry reportedly holding an open knife, and a row broke out at once. The Union's correspondent wrote that he could not learn what Henry said or did, or who fired the first shot, only that it was fired inside the building. In the fighting Jim Turner fired twice at Quinn, missing him but powder-burning a young man nearby.

Henry Turner was killed in the courthouse hall, Jim Turner jumped from a window and was shot on the square about thirty yards southeast of the building, and Rube Turner was killed in front of McGuire & Co.'s store. A few of the Black men returned fire, but most scattered when the whites began shooting. The Union's tally was three Turners killed outright, several other Black men wounded, two white men "very slightly wounded," and one powder-burned in the eye.

No inquest, arrest or prosecution for the killings appears in the coverage, and none of the white men who fired is named. When the Hernando County circuit court met that fall, the Brooksville Crescent reported that no case was tried and the grand jury found only two bills, "for minor offences."

Every surviving account came from white correspondents writing for Jacksonville papers. The first Brooksville dispatch, quoted in the Savannah Morning News on July 1, called the dead "members of the notorious Turner gang." The fuller Union letter, reprinted by the same paper on July 4 as "The Riot at Brooksville," spoke of "armed and turbulent negroes," praised the "well directed shots of the whites," and closed by crediting "the utmost forbearance on the part of the whites" for holding off a two-year-old difficulty.

A condensed Jacksonville wire ran in papers from Maine to Utah between July 3 and mid-July, under headlines such as "Conflict of Races" and "A War of Races." It repeated that one of the Turners had started the row by entering the courthouse with an open knife, a detail the Brooksville correspondent himself did not claim to know. Smaller papers reduced the story to a line in crime columns; the Lake Charles Echo wrote that the three had "opened the ball" in the courthouse, and the Crawford Avalanche called it "a riot between whites and blacks" and noted the dead were "all brothers."

The first dispatch reported two dead, "Henry Turner and Jim Rube," and one white man wounded, while the Union letter and all later reports gave three dead brothers. Counts of the wounded also varied: the Lake Charles Echo gave four Black men badly wounded and two or three whites, other wire items said "several" on each side.

reader.title: Brooksville courthouse shooting
bases: White townspeople, with a marshal and newly appointed special police on hand, fired on a party of armed Black men at the courthouse and square, killing three Turner brothers and wounding several others in what the papers called a 'riot' and a 'conflict of races' (A6, A3, A21).

A Thursday special from Brooksville (A1) and a separate, fuller Brooksville letter in the Jacksonville Union (A6) agree on the core event, a courthouse fight in which members of the Turner family were killed, and every wire summary repeats it (A2, A3, A5, A13); all reports, however, come from the white side through Jacksonville papers.

accounts.label: Jacksonville Union correspondent at Brooksville
accounts.gist: After a week of quarrels and arrests, armed Black men filled the town; when court was called Jim and Henry Turner entered, a row began, and the whites shot down all three brothers; the writer could not learn who fired first.

accounts.label: Wire summary

framing.detail: The Union letter blamed 'armed and turbulent negroes', credited 'the utmost forbearance on the part of the whites', and praised their 'well directed shots'; the first dispatch called the victims 'the notorious Turner gang'.
Northern papers ran the Jacksonville wire under 'Conflict of Races' and 'A War of Races' or as one line in crime columns, repeating that a Turner started the row with an open knife.

conflicts.note: The later, fuller Union letter names all three and where each died; 'Jim Rube' in the first dispatch looks like a running together of two names.
